rationale: The scenario is a straightforward HazCom applicability case: employer uses a hazardous chemical, decants it into workplace containers, and has employees not previously trained. This triggers the written hazard communication program requirement, SDS availability, container labeling (with the exception for immediate-use transfer containers noted), and the requirement to train employees on new chemical hazards before/at time of introduction. PSM provisions do not apply absent facts indicating a 'highly hazardous chemical' process covered by 1910.119.

The scenario describes a new technician assignment to a covered PSM process prior to startup of duties. §1910.119(i)(2) requires pre-startup safety review confirming training of each employee involved in operating the process has been completed. §1910.1200(h)(1) requires HazCom training at initial assignment, with content requirements specified in (h)(3). These are directly triggered by onboarding/process assignment; no conflicting facts require escalation, and the necessary facts (new assignment, covered process, employee status) are present.

The scenario describes a non-replacement-in-kind modification to process equipment/technology that changes process safety information, followed by introduction of highly hazardous chemicals and restart. This squarely triggers PSM management of change requirements (l)(1) and (l)(4) requiring updated process safety information, the pre-startup safety review (i)(2) which must confirm MOC compliance and training before introducing highly hazardous chemicals, updates to process safety information (d), operating procedure review for changes in equipment/technology (f)(3), and HazCom training obligations for employees facing newly introduced chemical hazards (h)(1) and (h)(3). These are directly supported by the stated facts without need for additional information.

The scenario describes a near-miss that could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic release of a highly hazardous chemical at a PSM-covered process. This directly triggers the incident investigation requirement under 1910.119(m)(1), which mandates investigation of incidents that resulted in or could reasonably have resulted in a catastrophic release, regardless of whether an injury occurred. No fatality, hospitalization, amputation, or loss of eye is reported, so OSHA recordkeeping reporting thresholds (1904.39) are not triggered. Contractor-related PSM provisions are not clearly implicated since no contractor-specific hazard exposure or injury is described.

With 300 employees, the establishment exceeds the 250-employee threshold under §1904.41(a)(1)(ii), triggering mandatory electronic submission of Form 300A. The establishment must also complete the standard year-end recordkeeping cycle: recording work-related injuries/illnesses (§1904.4(a), §1904.31(a)), entering them within 7 days (§1904.29(b)(3)), creating and certifying the annual summary (§1904.32(a)(2)-(3)), posting it (§1904.32(a)(4), §1904.32(b)(5)), and retaining records for five years (§1904.33(a)). The 20-249 employee electronic submission rule (REC-026) does not apply since the establishment exceeds 249 employees and falls under the 250+ threshold instead.

The scenario concerns the approaching anniversary of the last review of a machine-specific energy control procedure, which directly triggers the periodic inspection requirement under §1910.147(c)(6)(i), requiring an annual inspection of the energy control procedure to ensure compliance. No conflicting facts or missing predicates are present; this is a straightforward periodic review scenario governed by the cited requirement.

Maintenance employees entering a machine to clear a jam constitutes servicing/maintenance where unexpected startup or release of stored pneumatic energy could occur, squarely triggering the LOTO standard. This requires an established energy control program with documented procedures (c)(4)(i), isolation and rendering inoperative (c)(1), physical isolation of energy sources (d)(3), relief of stored/residual pneumatic energy (d)(5)(i), and training on the program (c)(7)(i). No facts indicate outside contractors, job/process changes, or PSM-covered highly hazardous chemicals, so those provisions are not applicable here.

The scenario describes a contractor being selected to work in a covered PSM process area for the first time, which directly triggers OSHA's contractor provisions under 1910.119(h): evaluating contractor safety performance before selection, informing the contractor of process hazards, ensuring contract employees are trained on those hazards, maintaining a contractor injury/illness log, and developing safe work practices governing contractor entrance/exit/presence in process areas. These requirements are all explicitly supported by the scenario facts (contractor entering process area for first time, facing fire/explosion/toxic release hazards).

The scenario is squarely governed by §1904.35(b)(2)(v)(A), which requires an employer to provide a former employee a copy of their own OSHA 301 Incident Report by the end of the next business day upon request. This provision directly and completely answers the scenario without need for additional facts or escalation.

The scenario matches §1904.35(b)(2)(v)(B) exactly: an authorized employee representative requesting OSHA 301 Incident Reports for represented employees at an establishment. The employer must provide copies within 7 calendar days, but only the 'Tell us about the case' section, with all other information redacted.

A work-related employee fatality triggers the 8-hour OSHA fatality reporting requirement under §1904.39(a)(1), and the case must also be recorded per the general recording criteria in §1904.4(a) and §1904.7(a), since death is an explicit recordability criterion.

The scenario describes a work-related amputation with in-patient hospitalization, learned of today. This is a clear recordable case under §1904.4(a) and §1904.7(a) (medical treatment beyond first aid, and specifically amputation/hospitalization). It must be entered on the OSHA 300 Log/301 within 7 calendar days per §1904.29(b)(3), and separately reported to OSHA within 24 hours per §1904.39(a)(2) due to the amputation and hospitalization triggers. No conflicting facts or missing predicates exist; the facts are sufficient to determine the applicable recordkeeping and reporting obligations.

The scenario involves a new employee informed of injury reporting procedures per §1904.35(b)(1)(ii), and a supervisor threatening discipline after an injury report, which directly implicates the anti-retaliation provision §1904.35(b)(1)(iv) and the reasonable-procedure requirement §1904.35(b)(1)(i), since threats of discipline could deter reporting. These provisions are clearly applicable and supported by the facts given.

The scenario describes a triennial PSM compliance audit that identified deficiencies requiring corrective action. This directly maps to the compliance audit requirements under 1910.119(o): certification of triennial audits (o)(1), audit conducted by a knowledgeable person (o)(2), prompt determination and documentation of response to findings and correction of deficiencies (o)(4), and retention of the two most recent audit reports (o)(5). These requirements are fully supported by the provided excerpts and directly applicable to the scenario without need for additional facts.

The scenario directly involves process equipment inspection under PSM finding a deficiency (pressure vessel outside acceptable limits). §1910.119(j)(4) requires documented inspection/testing of process equipment, and §1910.119(j)(5) requires correction of deficiencies outside acceptable limits before further use or in a safe and timely manner. These two requirements are squarely applicable and sufficient to answer the scenario without additional facts.

The scenario describes a failure of immediate SDS accessibility during a work shift, which is directly addressed by 1910.1200(g)(1) requiring SDS maintenance and (g)(8) requiring ready accessibility during each work shift including electronic access without barriers. These provisions are sufficient to determine the compliance gap without additional facts.

The scenario describes a portable container filled from a labeled drum and used immediately by the same employee who made the transfer, with no storage for later use. This squarely fits the labeling exemption in §1910.1200(f)(8), which exempts portable containers intended only for immediate use by the employee who performs the transfer from the general labeling requirement of (f)(6). No other HazCom requirements (training, SDS, program) are directly implicated by this specific transfer/labeling question.

rationale: The scenario describes a multi-employer worksite where one employer's hazardous chemicals may expose another employer's workers, which is directly addressed by the HazCom multi-employer provision requiring SDS access methods to be included in the written program, along with the underlying written program, chemical list, SDS availability, and access requirements. This is a determinate HazCom scenario not involving PSM-covered highly hazardous chemical processes, so PSM contractor provisions are not applicable absent evidence of a covered process.

This is exactly the type of technical equivalency judgment that determines whether MOC, PSSR, and related training/documentation obligations under §1910.119(l), (i), and LOTO retraining requirements are triggered. Because the facts conflict (engineering's characterization vs. maintenance records) and resolving this requires qualified engineering/safety judgment about technical equivalence, this cannot be resolved by rule application alone.

Determining whether this is truly a replacement in kind (exempt from MOC) or a change requiring full MOC/PSSR/training procedures requires qualified engineering evaluation of technical equivalency, which is not resolvable from the excerpts alone and requires human/expert escalation.

The scenario does not establish whether the illness was work-related or whether the hospitalization was for in-patient treatment, both of which are material predicates for triggering the reporting duty.

Without knowing the SDS classification of the product and whether it differs from previously trained hazard categories, it cannot be determined whether new training is legally required.
